summary: AstroBase is a free browser game where kids aged 7 to 12 run a base on Mars or the Moon and keep five astronauts alive for 30 days. One shared power supply feeds life support, heating, water recycling, a greenhouse and a science lab, so every choice costs something. Before each mission the game reads real space weather from NASA's DONKI database: a busy Sun means more solar storms, so the player must decide how much to invest in radiation shielding and a storm shelter. After every day, the game explains what changed, why it happened, and what to try next time, so failure teaches instead of punishing. Every number in the game is cited in an in-game Science Library. It needs no download and no account, and teachers can share one mission link so a whole class plays the same events.
details:
WHAT IT DOES: The player chooses Mars or the Moon, a difficulty, and the Sun conditions. Each turn is one day (a sol on Mars). The player sets power priorities, dims the greenhouse or lab, builds modules (solar panels, battery, water recycler, greenhouse, regolith shielding, storm shelter), gives the five crew members jobs and plans spacewalks. Events vary between runs: dust storms, lunar shadow periods, solar particle events, equipment failures, crop disease, crew illness and a resupply lander.

HOW IT WORKS: One shared power supply feeds life support, heating, water recycling, the greenhouse and the science lab. If solar power plus the battery cannot cover demand, systems are served in the player's priority order, and a system that gets 60% of its power produces 60% of its output. Oxygen is made by electrolysis (7 kWh per kg), water is recycled at 85 to 98%, greenhouse beds take 10 days to grow, and radiation comes from cosmic rays plus solar particle events, reduced by regolith shielding and the storm shelter. Every choice costs something: shielding early slows food and science, skipping it risks the radiation budget.

REAL NASA DATA: Before each mission the game calls NASA DONKI for the last 30 days of solar particle events and coronal mass ejections. Proton events seen by the GOES satellites and the number of coronal mass ejections set the sun level (Quiet, Active or Stormy), which multiplies the daily chance of a solar particle event by 0.5, 1 or 2. So the player's shielding decision follows what the real Sun is doing. If NASA cannot be reached, the game offers recorded DONKI periods (May 2024, October 2024, mid-2019, and the 60 days before the hackathon), always labelled with their dates and never presented as live. Life support values come from NASA BVAD, Mars radiation from Curiosity RAD, the career limit from NASA-STD-3001, water recovery from the ISS ECLSS, dust storms from NASA/JPL 2018 reports and lunar shadows from LOLA. All 114 values are listed in the in-game Science Library, marked as a sourced reference or a labelled game simplification.

LEARNING AND IMPACT: After every day a report shows a chain of causes, for example: dust storm, solar power down 58%, power short by 31 kWh, greenhouse lights cut, food grown down 1,320 kcal. The end-of-mission debrief gives a score, the turning point, and three lessons that start with what ended the mission, so failure teaches without punishing. Kids leave understanding a real deep-space constraint: solar storms are dangerous, forecasts matter, and shielding and shelters work. Teachers can create a class link so every student plays the same mission and the same recorded Sun, with a 30-minute lesson plan and discussion questions.

TOOLS: TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, dnd-kit, Recharts, Vitest, ESLint, GitHub Actions and Vercel. It runs in any modern browser with no download, no account and no tracking, and works offline once loaded. Accessibility: keyboard play, status shown with text as well as colour, large-text mode, reduced motion, and light and dark themes. Quality: 46 automated tests and a balance simulator that plays thousands of missions with three bots to keep the game hard but fair. All artwork is drawn in code; no NASA logos are used.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE: We used Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code, as a coding assistant for writing, testing and debugging code. The game design, trade-offs and data sources were chosen by the team, and the game was play-tested by the team.
